content: All studies were assessed to have an unclear risk of bias concerning the composite reference standard. This was due to the imperfect accuracy of the composite reference standard and the varying definitions of this standard used by the primary study authors. Regarding applicability in the patient selection domain, 50% of studies were judged to have a high or unclear risk of bias because participants were exclusively evaluated as inpatients at tertiary care centers, or the clinical setting was unclear. For the applicability of the index test, most studies (72%) were judged to have low concern due to the standardized application of the index tests. Eleven studies evaluating stool as a specimen for Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra were judged to have an unclear risk of bias due to the absence of a standardized protocol for stool preparation. The applicability of the reference standard was considered a low concern for most studies (93%). Six studies were included to generate evidence about the detection of rifampicin resistance. All six studies (223 participants) evaluated only Xpert MTB/RIF and were conducted in high TB burden and high MDR-TB burden countries. Among these studies, 50% had a low risk of bias concerning patient selection, while all studies had a low risk of bias concerning the reference standard. The risk of bias was considered low for the reference standard if an automated process was used or if it was clear that the reference standard results were interpreted without knowledge of the index tests. For all six studies, there were applicability concerns regarding patient selection because participants were enrolled exclusively from inpatient or tertiary care centers. For the meta-analysis, a total of 23 studies (6612 participants) evaluated sputum specimens; 14 studies (3468 participants) evaluated gastric specimens; four studies (1125 participants) evaluated nasopharyngeal specimens; and 11 studies (1592 participants) evaluated stool specimens. All these studies evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF alone. Three studies (753 participants) evaluated both Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra on frozen sputum specimens. One study (195 participants) evaluated both Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra on nasopharyngeal specimens. No studies evaluated Xpert Ultra alone for the diagnostic accuracy of pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance in children compared with MRS and CRS. Three studies (753 participants) evaluated both Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra on frozen sputum specimens. One study (195 participants) evaluated both Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra on nasopharyngeal specimens. For extrapulmonary TB, 65 studies were included. A total of 63 studies (13,144 participants) evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF, including five that evaluated both Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra. The included studies evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimens, lymph node aspirate, lymph node biopsy, pleural fluid, urine, synovial fluid, peritoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, and blood. Of the 65 studies, 39 (60%) were conducted in high TB burden countries, and 41 (63%) in high TB/HIV burden countries. Risk of bias was judged to be low in the domains of patient selection, index test, and flow and timing, but high or unclear in the reference standard domain because many studies decontaminated sterile specimens before culture inoculation. Regarding applicability, in the patient selection domain, high or unclear concern was expressed for most studies because participants were either evaluated exclusively as inpatients at tertiary care centers or the clinical settings were unclear. For lymph node TB diagnosis, six studies (210 participants) evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF against an MRS of smear or culture on lymph node specimens. Two studies (105 participants) evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF against a composite reference standard for lymph node TB. For TB meningitis, six studies (241 participants) evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF against culture on CSF. Additionally, two studies (155 participants) assessed Xpert MTB/RIF against a composite reference standard that included a clinical diagnosis of TB meningitis. The certainty of evidence was judged to be very low for sensitivity and low for specificity for the detection of both TB meningitis and lymph node TB. No studies evaluating the accuracy of Xpert Ultra for detecting lymph node TB or TB meningitis were identified. For pulmonary TB in adults, six surveys were identified. These surveys used sputum samples to evaluate Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra against the reference standard of culture for TB. The surveys evaluated the index tests in adults (aged ≥15 years) with chest X-ray abnormalities or symptoms suggestive of pulmonary TB (or both). The analysis reported on the results of four surveys, including 49,556 participants. The evidence was downgraded one level for indirectness and one level for inconsistency. The certainty of evidence was judged to be low for sensitivity and moderate for specificity. For repeated Xpert Ultra tests in adults with pulmonary TB symptoms, the analysis included data from three surveys with 5080 participants. Serious concerns were expressed about the indirectness of the evidence, as most data were from Myanmar, and the results may not be applicable to other settings. Very serious concerns were also expressed about imprecision due to the small number of individuals contributing to the analysis. The certainty of evidence was judged to be very low for sensitivity and moderate for specificity.
